newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.S. urges U.N. to encourage steps to Mideast peace.
newsitem.headline: U.S. urges U.N. to encourage steps to Mideast peace.

text.p: The United States urged the Security Council on Friday to encourage Israel and the Palestinians to revive the Middle East peace process and not to condemn Israel.

The call, by U.S. envoy Madeleine Albright, contrasted with the views of most other speakers, who criticised Israel in varying degrees for opening an archaeological tunnel in the Old City of Jerusalem and accused it of delaying moves toward peace.
"Let us turn our attention not toward condemnation but toward encouraging the parties to restore the peace process and return to efforts to achieve concrete progress," Albright told the council.

She had opposed holding the debate, sparked by violence that has claimed the lives of more than 50 Palestinians and over a dozen Israelis since Israel recently opened a new entrance to an undeground passage near the al-Aqsa mosque, Islam's third-holiest shrine.
Albright, whose country is the main sponsor of the peace process, said the first objective was to restore calm, then to accelerate the negotiating process.

"Words here are no substitute for action in the region," she said, alluding to U.S. efforts to prod Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat to meet and restore the peace momentum.
In Houston, White House spokesman Mike McCurry said President (Bill) Clinton was encouraged by reports the Israeli and Palestinian leaders were on the verge of a meeting.
They had not yet announced a meeting "but it could be soon and it could be over the weekend," McCurry said.

Syrian Foreign Minister Farouk al-Shara, in a particularly tough speech to the council, said: "The peace process is dying; the peace process might be buried and we might not have another opportunity such as the one we had to implement a comprehensive just peace in the Middle East."
Negotiations on the Syrian-Israel track have long been frozen, with Syria demanding the return of the entire Golan Heights, captured by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war.

Accusing Israel of "arrogance and intransigence," Shara said the council should not confine itself to the question of the tunnel "but should adopt the right resolution to save the peace process ...to save the area and the region from more violence, tension, which would benefit nobody."
It was "high time for Israel to realise that it will not be able to achieve peace and keep the occupied territories. It has to choose," he added.

Jordan's Minister of State for Foreign Affairs, Khaled al-Madadha, said his government had made persistent efforts to urge Israel's new prime minister to return to the framework of the peace negotiations.
"The serious bloody events that erupted lately have confirmed our apprehensions," he said.
He called for the closing of the tunnel and the establishment of an international committee, as proposed by Jodan's King Hussein, to deal with archaeological sites in Jerusalem.
"We Arabs and Israelis must rise to the level of the expectations of all ...peoples to achieve a lasting and just peace, based on peaceful principles upon wich we agreed," Madadha said.

Iranian Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati, whose country opposes the peace process and Israel's existence, said the crisis had shown the "real face of the Zionist regime disguised behind the facade of peace."
More than 40 speakers were taking part in the daylong debate but by evening no resolution had been formally proposed.

One Arab text serving as a basis for negotiation would condemn Israel's actions, demand the closing of the tunnel and call for the immediate resumption of the Middle East peace process and the implementation of agreements already reached.
The United States, as a permanent council member with a veto, can block any resolution or statement which it regards as unacceptable.
